title: Move all zeros to the end while preserving order (two-pointer swap).
shortTitle: Move All Zeros to the End While Preserving Order

s1_definition.profdef: Moving all zeros to the end while preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements is a two-pointer, in-place algorithm. A write pointer tracks where the next non-zero value should go, and a scan pointer walks the whole array; every time the scan pointer finds a non-zero value it is placed at the write position and the write pointer advances. After the scan, all positions from the write pointer to the end are filled with zeros. It is linear time and constant space, and the non-zero elements keep their original order, which is what makes it a stable partition.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a row of settlement slots for Rajesh's day, where some slots carry a real amount and some are empty, shown as zero. The bank wants all the real amounts compacted to the front in the same order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back. A clerk keeps a finger on the next front slot to fill and runs another finger across every slot; each real amount found is slid forward to the kept position, and whatever is left at the back becomes empty.
s1_definition.oneliner: Write pointer collects non-zeros in order at the front; fill the rest with zeros at the end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Moving all zeros to the end while preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements is a two-pointer, in-place algorithm. A write pointer tracks where the next non-zero value should go, and a scan pointer walks the whole array; every time the scan pointer finds a non-zero value it is placed at the write position and the write pointer advances. After the scan, all positions from the write pointer to the end are filled with zeros. It is linear time and constant space, and the non-zero elements keep their original order, which is what makes it a stable partition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a row of settlement slots for Rajesh's day, where some slots carry a real amount and some are empty, shown as zero. The bank wants all the real amounts compacted to the front in the same order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back. A clerk keeps a finger on the next front slot to fill and runs another finger across every slot; each real amount found is slid forward to the kept position, and whatever is left at the back becomes empty.

**One line to remember:** Write pointer collects non-zeros in order at the front; fill the rest with zeros at the end.

sections.s2_technical:
The classic two-pass version is the easiest to reason about. In the first pass you keep a write index starting at zero and scan the array; each time you see a non-zero value you store it at the write index and increment the write index. After this pass, the first write-index positions hold all the non-zero values in their original relative order. In the second step you fill every position from the write index to the end with zero. Both passes are linear, so the whole thing is linear time.

There is a one-pass swap variant. You keep the write index and scan; when you find a non-zero value you swap it with the value at the write index and advance the write index. This moves zeros rightward as you go. It does more writes than the fill version when there are many zeros because of the swaps, but it is a single pass and is common in interviews. I usually mention both and note that the fill version does fewer writes when zeros are frequent.

A critical requirement is stability: the non-zero values must keep their original order. Both the write-and-fill and the swap approaches preserve order because they process elements left to right and never reorder two non-zeros relative to each other. If you instead swapped from both ends you would be faster at moving zeros but you would scramble the order of the non-zeros, which violates the requirement.

A senior point is minimising writes. If the array is mostly non-zero, you want to avoid writing a value back onto itself. A small optimisation skips the store when the write index already equals the scan index, which avoids redundant self-writes and slightly reduces memory traffic on large arrays. For a banking batch over millions of slots this is a measurable saving.

Another senior point is generality. The same pattern is a stable partition around any predicate, not just zero. By replacing the non-zero test with any condition, you push all elements failing the predicate to the end while keeping the passing ones in order, which is a reusable building block. For money I use BigDecimal and test compareTo against zero rather than the equality operator.

A small finance-domain example: `int write = 0; for (int scan = 0; scan < a.length; scan++) { if (a[scan].signum() != 0) { a[write++] = a[scan]; } } while (write < a.length) { a[write++] = BigDecimal.ZERO; }` compacts non-zero amounts to the front and zeros to the back.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes Rajesh's daily settlement slots, where many slots are empty placeholders holding zero and the rest hold real transaction amounts. A reporting module must present the real amounts compacted to the front in the exact order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back, and it must do this in place to avoid allocating a second array for a very large day. Moving zeros to the end while preserving order is exactly this stable compaction.

This is exactly how move-zeros works in Java — a write pointer gathers the non-zero amounts in order and the tail is filled with zeros.

Problem 2 — The order of the real amounts is audit-significant, so the compaction must be stable: two real amounts must never swap their relative positions. This rules out the faster two-ends swap and requires the left-to-right write approach, and amounts are BigDecimal so the zero test uses signum rather than equals.

What the code will do: a `SlotCompactor` with `moveZerosToEnd(BigDecimal[] slots)` using the write-and-fill two-pointer approach with signum, preserving order. The demo compacts Rajesh's day of settlement slots and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the slots are `5000, 0, 12000, 0, 0, 800`.

Step 1: write starts at zero. scan at index zero finds `5000`, which is non-zero. write equals scan, so no redundant copy; write advances to one.

Step 2: scan at index one finds `0`. It is zero, so nothing happens and write stays at one.

Step 3: scan at index two finds `12000`, non-zero. write is one and scan is two, so we copy `12000` into position one. The array front is now `5000, 12000`. write advances to two.

Step 4: scan at indices three and four both find `0`, so nothing happens and write stays at two. scan at index five finds `800`, non-zero, so we copy `800` into position two. The front is now `5000, 12000, 800`. write advances to three.

Step 5: The scan ends. All non-zero amounts have been written to the front in their original order, preserving the audit-significant sequence. write is three, meaning three real amounts.

Step 6: We fill the tail from position three to the end with zero, giving `5000, 12000, 800, 0, 0, 0`. The compaction is stable and done entirely in place with no second array.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:30:00Z INFO Before: [5000, 0, 12000, 0, 0, 800]
2026-10-26T16:30:00Z INFO Compacted slots: [5000, 12000, 800, 0, 0, 0]
2026-10-26T16:30:00Z INFO After (non-zeros front, order kept): [5000, 12000, 800, 0, 0, 0]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Moving all zeros to the end while preserving order is a two-pointer in-place algorithm. I keep a write pointer for the next front position and scan the whole array; every non-zero value I find I place at the write position and advance the write pointer, then after the scan I fill everything from the write pointer to the end with zeros. It is linear time and constant space.

The requirement I never lose sight of is stability: the non-zero values must keep their original relative order. Both the write-and-fill version and the one-pass swap version preserve order because they process left to right and never reorder two non-zeros. A faster two-ends approach would move zeros quicker but scramble the non-zeros, which breaks the requirement, so I avoid it when order matters.

I also mention a small optimisation: skip the store when the write index already equals the scan index, which avoids pointless self-writes on a mostly-non-zero array and reduces memory traffic on large inputs. And I note that this is really a stable partition around a predicate, so replacing the non-zero test with any condition reuses the same code; for money I test BigDecimal with signum rather than equals.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to compact Rajesh's daily settlement slots, pushing the empty zero slots to the back while keeping the real amounts in the exact order they occurred, because that order is audit-significant. It runs in place to avoid allocating a second array for a huge day, and the zero test uses signum because amounts are BigDecimal. Explaining the stability requirement, the two approaches, and the self-write optimisation shows the interviewer that I understand in-place partitioning and respect the ordering constraint that the business actually depends on.
